newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Anti-APEC leftists play cat and mouse with police.
newsitem.headline: Anti-APEC leftists play cat and mouse with police.

text.p: Hundreds of demonstrators scattered through the streets of Manila on Thursday after police blocked an anti-APEC march to the presidential palace.

As ministers flew into the Philippines to prepare for Monday's summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, demonstrators, with a handful of Roman Catholic priests in the forefront, tried to march through central Manila.

Riot police stopped the demonstrators, some of whom wore masks of U.S. President Bill Clinton and Philippine President Fidel Ramos, after only a few metres (yards) of their eight km (five mile) journey. Police said the marchers needed a permit.

For about two hours there was a stand-off. The demonstrators -- peasants, students, trade unionists and even a few nuns -- sang and danced in the street, creating traffic gridlock over a large part of the capital, while armed riot police looked on.
Suddenly, the demonstrators began running. Chanting, whistling and banging drums, they fanned out through side streets in a bid to outflank the police and reach the palace.

Baton-wielding police gave chase and managed to stop them before they reached the palace, although some got to within a few blocks of their goal. Two protesters were arrested, leaders of the demonstration said.
Roman Catholic priests supporting the protest said the marchers were particularly angry over the clearance of thousands of slum dwellers from shantytowns ahead of the APEC meeting.
"The government thought they were an eyesore, but many of the poor now have no homes," said Fransciscan priest Greg Redoblado.
Leaders said the demonstration was the first in a series of protests against the APEC summit in Subic Bay on Monday which aims to make progress towards creating the world's biggest free trade region.
Tens of thousands more Filipinos would take part in a series of demonstrations and strikes over the next four days, they said.
Clinton, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and leaders from other APEC states will attend the summit.
If the demonstrators' plans are realised it will be the biggest display of popular discontent with APEC since the grouping was conceived in 1989 to nurture the economic growth of the Pacific Rim.
Objectors say the organisation amounts to little more than a club to help big business exploit the underprivileged.

Across town more than 200 delegates from 34 countries began a three-day meeting in a suburban hotel to object to what they said was the failure of rich capitalist nations to share the fruits of economic progress with the poor.
Peasant leaders from Mexico, trade unionists from Canada and a group of Filipina nuns accused APEC of creating poverty and unemployment and destroying the fabric of native communities.
"Our call here is 'junk APEC'," said Satur Ocampo, spokesman for the People's Conference Against Imperialist Globalisation.

Nathaniel Santiago, secretary-general of the leftist labour alliance Bagong Alyansang Makabayan, said delegates would join a motorcade of 20,000 people from Manila to Subic on Sunday to protest against the summit at the former U.S. naval base.
He predicted that some 200,000 people would join in nationwide protests including transport and other strikes on the day of the summit.
